summary: This document updates the IPv6 multicast addressing architecture by redefining the reserved bits as generic flag bits, with some clarifications on using them. It updates RFCs 3956, 3306 and 4291.

eli5.summary: An address has a few spare switches in it that were never used. This RFC says those switches can be used as general flags and explains how to treat them.

questions: what are ipv6 multicast flag bits
what is ff2 in ipv6 multicast
subtitle: Turns the reserved bits of IPv6 multicast addresses into general flag bits and fixes the older RFCs that assumed otherwise.

tldr.problem: Bits 17-20 of an IPv6 multicast address were reserved in RFC 3306 and RFC 3956, and some implementations treat the flag bits as one 4-bit number, which makes it hard to give the remaining flags a meaning.
tldr.mechanism: The reserved bits become a second flag field, ff2, the original flags become ff1, and implementations MUST treat flag bits as separate bits. Affected text in RFC 3306 and RFC 3956 is rewritten.
tldr.outcome: Flag bits now apply to any multicast address and can be defined in the future, and examples such as the ffbx::/32 SSM range and the fff0::/12 Embedded-RP prefix become valid.

today: RFC 7371 is a Proposed Standard from September 2014 and, per the metadata, has not been obsoleted or updated. It updates RFC 3306, RFC 3956 and RFC 4291.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
This document updates the IPv6 addressing architecture of RFC 4291 by redefining reserved bits as generic flag bits. It also clarifies how those flags are used. It updates RFC 3956, RFC 3306 and RFC 4291, and these updates are logical consequences of the new processing rules.

IPv6 addresses in the RFC text follow the recommendation of RFC 5952.
sections.eli5: This RFC changes the rulebook for special group-mailing addresses so that some unused switches can be used later.

sections.title: The Address Layout Update
sections.content:
Bits 17-20 of a multicast address, counting bit 1 as the most significant, are reserved in RFC 3956 and RFC 3306. This document defines them as generic flag bits for any multicast address and calls them ff2 (flag field 2). The flgs bits in RFC 4291 are renamed ff1 (flag field 1).

This lets addresses be treated uniformly and lets the bits be defined later for different purposes, whatever the type of multicast address. The design was initially triggered by a Work in Progress that proposed giving one reserved bit a meaning. That draft also considered the last remaining flag in ff1, but this was abandoned because it is unclear whether there are other usage scenarios.
sections.eli5: The address has two rows of four switches. The first row keeps its job, and the second row is now open for future use.

sections.title: Flag Bits Are Separate Bits
sections.content:
Some implementations and specifications use the flag bits together as a 4-bit integer, which is a hurdle to giving the remaining bits a meaning. For example, reading RFC 3306 may suggest that ff3x::/32 is the only allowed Source-Specific Multicast (SSM) prefix block. RFC 3956 says only ff70::/12 applies to Embedded-RP.

The new requirement is short: implementations MUST treat flag bits as separate bits.
sections.eli5: Look at each switch by itself instead of reading the whole row as one number.

sections.title: Changes to RFC 3306
sections.content:
The address format in section 4 of RFC 3306 becomes: 8 bits of 11111111, ff1 (4 bits), scop (4 bits), ff2 (4 bits), rsvd (4 bits), plen (8 bits), a 64-bit network prefix and a 32-bit group ID.

The ff1 flags are XYPT. X and Y may each be 0 or 1; X is for future assignment and Y has a meaning in RFC 3956. The P and T rules stay: P = 1 means the address is assigned based on the network prefix, and then T MUST be 1. The four ff2 bits are rrrr; they MUST each be sent as zero and MUST be ignored on receipt.

Section 6 changes too. When ff1 is 0011, the SSM range is ff3x::/32, but it is not the only one: if the most significant ff1 bit is set, the range is ffbx::/32.
sections.eli5: The old description is rewritten so that the first row has four named switches and the second row is spare and must be left off for now.

sections.title: Changes to RFC 3956 (Embedded-RP)
sections.content:
RFC 3956 embeds the address of a Rendezvous Point (RP) in a multicast address. Its format is updated to use ff1 and ff2, and its ff1 flags are XRPT, where X may be 0 or 1. Before, only ff70::/12 counted as Embedded-RP and fff0::/12 was left unspecified.

Now R = 1 indicates an embedded RP address. P MUST be 1 and so T MUST be 1. This implies that, for instance, ff70::/12 and fff0::/12 are both embedded RP prefixes. When the R bit is set, the last 4 bits of the field reserved in RFC 3306 carry the RP interface ID.

The validity rule in section 4 now says the address MUST have the R-bit set and, for this embedding, P and T both set to 1. The longest-match rule in section 7.1 applies to addresses with the R-bit set to 1, not just FF70::/12.
sections.eli5: One of the switches means 'the meeting point is hidden inside this address'. The rule now follows that switch, not a fixed pattern.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
This document adds no new security text. The same security considerations as in RFC 3956, RFC 3306 and RFC 4291 are to be taken into account.

It is a Standards Track document, and it assigns no meaning to the new ff2 bits; they must be sent as zero and ignored on receipt.
sections.eli5: Nothing new to worry about. The safety rules from the older documents still apply.
